title: The dice-master's last day
hook: the patient brother faces Shalya, and the dice-master meets Sahadeva
carry: dharma is restored, in its own time
tomorrow: the last king is alone. where does he go?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Duryodhana turned down Kripa's plea for peace, and Shalya took command. Your line was it is never too late to turn toward dharma.

Who should face Shalya? On the Pandava side, the question goes to Krishna, and his answer is not the obvious one. Not Arjuna. Not Bhima. Yudhishthira: the eldest brother, the one who lost everything at dice, the one Karna sent back to camp humiliated just the day before. Shalya is strong, Krishna says, in effect, and you are the one to meet him. Put away your gentleness for today. And Yudhishthira, the man the epic keeps showing us as patient, picks up his weapons.
screen: `WHO SHOULD FACE SHALYA?` → `NOT ARJUNA. NOT BHIMA.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA.`

segments.voice: The fight is long and fierce, and in Ganguli's English the patient king is almost unrecognizable: steady, fearless, pressing forward. At last Yudhishthira hurls a dart, a spear made for throwing, with all his strength. It strikes Shalya, and the king of Madra falls. The twins have lost their uncle. As Shalya's army breaks, another fight finishes something older. Shakuni, Duryodhana's uncle, the man who threw the dice in the rigged game, is still on the field. In the dice hall, years before, the youngest brother Sahadeva had sworn that Shakuni would die by his hand. Now Sahadeva finds him. The dice-master has no dice here, and the vow from that hall is kept. Twelve years in the forest, a year in hiding, eighteen days of war, and the wrong done at a gaming table is finally answered. Many Hindus hear a teaching in a day like this. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back in its place. Notice what that promises, and what it doesn't. Not that wrong never wins: Shakuni won, for years. Only that it doesn't get the last word. Hindus hold on to that when cheating seems to pay. Dharma is restored, in its own time, not always in ours. And Duryodhana, looking around, finds himself almost alone.
screen: `SHALYA FALLS` · `SAHADEVA FINDS SHAKUNI` · `AGE AFTER AGE, DHARMA RESTORED` · then, large: `WRONG DOESN'T GET THE LAST WORD`

segments.voice: Sit tall and let your face soften. Bring to mind one wrong that seems to be winning, in your life or in the news, and don't rehearse the anger. If you pray, hand it to God, the way Hindus lean on Krishna's promise, and ask for patience and for the part that's yours to do. If you don't pray, name one small thing you can do for what's right, and leave the rest for now.
Shalya. The commander who falls to the patient eldest brother, while Sahadeva settles an old vow with the dice-master Shakuni.
Your line: dharma is restored, in its own time. The quiet brother remembered. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Yudhishthira's battle with Shalya and Sahadeva's killing of Shakuni are told in the Shalya Parva and in retellings and serials of the Mahabharata, as the moment the war's last vows begin to be kept.

fork.reveal: Shakuni's rigged win held for years and still didn't get the last word. the Gita's promise is that dharma comes back; your part is to keep it meanwhile.

chat.meaning: Shakuni's rigged dice won for years, and Sahadeva still answered them on the last day. In the Gita, Krishna promises to restore dharma whenever it declines, age after age.

tie.story: Shakuni won everything with rigged dice, and years later Sahadeva kept his vow from that hall on the war's last day.
